newsitem.title: FRANCE: RTRS - Australia and France end bitter nuclear row.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia and France end bitter nuclear row.

text.p: Australia and France said on Monday they were putting their differences behind them and ending a bitter row over French nuclear testing in the South Pacific.
"I think we have now a new basis for a new relationship between Australia and France," French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said after meeting Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
"The circumstances are different now and the mood is very good," Juppe told reporters.
"It was a good opportunity for us to revitalise our bilateral relations and we've gone a long way towards that today," Downer said after meeting French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
De Charette said the meetings had enabled the two nations "to turn the page and write together a fresh account of the friendship between France and Australia."
Foreign Ministry officials said de Charette had accepted an invitation from Downer to visit Australia. The visit probably will take place next year but no date has been set, they said.
"One of the purposes of my visit is to re-invigorate the Australia-France relationship and restore the momentum it had prior to the period of nuclear testing,"

Downer, the most senior Australian representative to visit Paris since the tests, told a lunch of the Australian Business in Europe (ABIE) group that a main purpose of his visit was to "re-invigorate the Australia-France relationship and restore the momentum it had prior to the period of nuclear testing".

At the height of the row, Australia's then prime minister Paul Keating branded as "an act of stupidity" tests ordered by President Jacques Chirac to upgrade France's nuclear arsenal before abolishing testing forever.
Australia accused France of acting as a colonial power in the South Pacific, while Paris said Australia was seizing on the tests to try and drive France out of the region.

"Australia welcomes, and indeed encourages, France increasing its links with the Asia-Pacific region," Downer said. "It is important that our two countries work together to ensure the continued stability and economic development of the region."
After carrying out its last test in January, Paris announced it was closing down its nuclear test range in French Polynesia.
It has since signed the Treaty of Rarotonga, making the South Pacific a nuclear-free zone, and announced it would sign a U.N. treaty outlawing all nuclear testing on September 24.
A conservative government took over in Australia last March from Labour, which had led the protests against the tests.
Downer said Australians had been "understandably upset", but a long-standing bilateral relationship could weather such rows.
"French investors are welcome in Australia...There are great opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region for countries such as France," he said.
French officials have described relations as convalescent and said they expected Downer's visit to seal reconciliation.

Trade and investment were apparently unscathed despite some calls on both sides for boycotts. Overall French exports to Australia rose during the period the tests were carried out, but some high-profile goods like wine suffered.
Most Australian exports to France, like uranium, coal and wool, are sold on long-term contracts and were unaffected.
Signalling a drive to boost Australian exports to France, Downer said trade was running very much in France's favour.
"Australia therefore naturally wants to do more and expand the range of Australian products and services to France."
French exports to Australia totalled 6.4 billion francs ($1.3 billion) in 1995, well above imports worth 4.4 billion francs ($854 million).
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
